title: The Story of the Odyssey
author: Alfred J. Church
openingText: When the great city of Troy had been taken, all the chiefs who had fought against it set sail for their homes. But there was wrath in heaven against them, so that they did not find a safe and happy return.
about:
Alfred John Church (1829–1912) retold Homer’s Odyssey for young readers. The story opens with Telemachus searching for news of his father while suitors consume the household of Ulysses on Ithaca. It then follows Ulysses himself, held on Calypso’s island, wrecked near the Phaeacians, and telling the tale of his ten years of wandering: the Cyclops, Circe, the dead, the Sirens, Scylla, and the cattle of the Sun.

The last third of the book is the return: Ulysses in disguise in his own home, recognised by his old nurse, winning the contest of the bow, and clearing his hall. The text uses the Latin name Ulysses throughout. This is a retelling in plain English prose and not a translation of the Greek.

whyItMatters.title: A journey told by the traveler
whyItMatters.body: Ulysses tells the tales of the Cyclops, Circe and the Sirens himself, as a guest at a feast. The poem therefore puts a storyteller inside the story and asks the reader to weigh what he says. The method has been copied by many later stories of homecoming.

whyItMatters.title: Hospitality is a test
whyItMatters.body: Strangers are fed and welcomed by the Phaeacians and the swineherd Eumaeus, and abused by the suitors. Who treats a guest well reveals who deserves to rule. The question still applies to how a household or a country treats those who arrive without power.

whyItMatters.title: Cunning against strength
whyItMatters.body: Ulysses wins by disguise, patience and trickery as much as by force. He hides his name from the Cyclops and his face from his own household. Readers can compare him with heroes who simply fight.

angleCards.title: Track the disguises
angleCards.text: Notice every time Ulysses hides who he is, and what he gains or risks by doing so.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Story of the Odyssey to follow how disguise and concealed identity shape Ulysses’ return.

angleCards.title: Compare the hosts
angleCards.text: Set the Phaeacians, Eumaeus and the suitors side by side and ask how each treats a stranger.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Story of the Odyssey to compare how different hosts treat Ulysses.

angleCards.title: Follow Telemachus
angleCards.text: Watch how Telemachus changes between the assembly in the first chapters and the slaying of the suitors.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Story of the Odyssey to see how Telemachus grows into his father’s son.

angleCards.title: Weigh the monsters
angleCards.text: Read the Cyclops, Circe and the Sirens as tests and ask what each one tests.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Story of the Odyssey to understand what each monster and enchantress tests in Ulysses.
